newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Oct 4.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Oct 4.

text.p: Prepared by The Broadcast Monitoring Company for Reuters

-- MORE NORTH SEA FIELDS TO CLOSE Due to dwindling reserves, another 14 North Sea oil and gas fields are lined up for closure over the coming three years. A report out today from consultants Wood Mackenzie estimates the total cost of closing fields and removing installations from all North Sea fields will be around 8.7 billion pounds stg, representing 123 million pounds stg on average for the 71 companies involved in offshore operations.

-- HAMLEYS CHIEF RESIGNS AS PROFITS SURGE 18 PER CENT The chief executive of Hamleys, Geoff Cullinan, has resigned after only six months in his job. Hamleys, the toy shop, said that the departure was amicable, and Mr Cullinan will be paid compensation but the amount has yet to be settled. Hamleys also reported an 18 percent rise to 2 million pounds stg in pre-tax profits for the six months to July.

-- ASW SEEKS BUYER FOR RECYCLING DIVISION ASW, the Cardiff-based steelmaker, is seeking a buyer for its British metal recycling business in a bid to reduce its debts. The recycling business operates from 12 sites in Britain. SBC Warburg has been appointed to lead the search. It was stressed that the recycling operations had sales of 75 million pounds stg in 1995 and had been profitable over the last three years.

-- BRITISH GAS REJECTS PRICE CUTS British Gas has rejected a new price formula for Transco, its pipeline business forcing Ofgas, the industry regulator, to refer the pricing issue to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission. British Gas said the new formula would lead to a 400 million pound stg drop in annual revenues. The move comes after months of negotiations between Ofgas and British Gas over the pricing formula. Ofgas's initial proposals included a price cut of 20 percent. Gas consumers will now have to wait an extra six months for a proposed cut in their annual bills.

-- STOCK EXCHANGE UNVEILS REFORMS The London Stock Exchange yesterday revealed plans to introduce the most radical changes to the way in which shares in the top 100 companies are traded since the Big Bang. The new system will involve investors placing orders through Stock Exchange member firms, such as stockbrokers and the orders will then be placed on a universal order book and the buy or sell instruction being executed at the best possible price. The new system will create a level playing field and not just favour the professional traders.

-- POWER STRUGGLE LOOMS FOR GRID A power struggle between the National Grid and the electricity regulator, Offer, looks increasingly likely to go to the Monopolies and Mergers commission as the watchdog stuck to its stance on transmission price controls. The proposals mean that customers will benefit by almost 1 billion pounds stg over the next four years, or an annual saving of around 4 pounds stg on every 300 pounds stg bill. National Grid is refusing to comment in detail, but has until October 30 to respond. Analysts say that there is an even chance that it will seek an MMC inquiry.

-- OLIVETTI SELL-OFF TO RAISE 520 MILLION POUNDS Olivetti is to raise up to 520 million pounds through disposals and the flotation of its Lexikon office equipment business, over the next two years. The troubled Italian technology group is aiming to sell four businesses by the end of this year including the personal computer division which has been the main cause of the group's misfortunes.

-- VIRGIN SEEKS TO BUILD AIR NETWORK IN AFRICA Richard Branson, speaking after the inaugural flight of Virgin Atlantic's service between London and Johannesburg, said he wanted to buy Sun Air, the South African state-owned airline as a base for a continent-wide network on the model of his new Virgin Express short-haul airline in Europe.

-- CLOTHING RETAILERS COUNTER SWEATSHOP CLAIMS C&A and Marks & Spencer yesterday countered claims of sweatshop conditions in their British factories. C&A said it had called its inspectors in to two suppliers in Birmingham warning them about safety risks and also rejected claims that some workers were paid less than 2 pounds stg an hour. Britain's biggest clothing chain, Marks & Spencer said it was confident that its suppliers met high standards.

-- P&O AND STENA COMBINE FORCES TO TAKE ON TUNNEL Chairman of P&O Lord Sterling, yesterday agreed to a 410 million pounds stg merger of its Dover-to-Calais ferry business with Stena of Sweden. He predicted that the deal would mean no price rises on cross-Channel routes but would mean big job cuts. The move, which brings together the two biggest ferry operators on the busiest part of the Channel, is the latest and most dramatic step taken yet by ferry companies to combat the price war started by the opening of the Channel Tunnel.

-- ROSS PLANS BOARD RESTRUCTURING AT LITTLEWOODS GROUP A big shake-up of the Littlewoods board structure is planned by James Ross, the new chairman of the retail and football pools group. The move could see the last remaining members of the controlling Moores family leave the board. Mr Ross is confident that the changes can be made with the family's agreement. The changes will include the creation of three categories of director: executive; non-executive; and link directors.

-- DBS HALTS PLANS FOR FULL LISTING DBS Management have shelved plans to move from the Alternative Investment Market to a full stock-market listing. The network for independent financial advisers admitted that it faced a series of allegations from its former compliance director. DBS have asked the Personal Investment Authority to investigate the allegations, and stressed that the allegations did not place investors' funds at rusk. Shares in DBS fell sharply from 481p to 422.5p.
